claim: The hand area of the primary somatosensory cortex contains detailed finger topography.
source: The hand area of the primary somatosensory cortex contains detailed finger topography, thought to be shaped and maintained by daily life experience.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Finger topography in the primary somatosensory cortex is thought to be shaped and maintained by daily life experience.
source: The hand area of the primary somatosensory cortex contains detailed finger topography, thought to be shaped and maintained by daily life experience.
evidence: This is presented as a prevailing theory in the field.

claim: Representation of the missing hand's individual fingers persists in the primary somatosensory cortex even decades after arm amputation.
source: We show that representation of the missing hand's individual fingers persists in the primary somatosensory cortex even decades after arm amputation.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by neuroimaging data from amputees.

claim: The discovery of persistent digit topography of amputees' missing hand could be exploited for the development of intuitive and fine-grained control of neuroprosthetics.
source: The discovery of persistent digit topography of amputees' missing hand could be exploited for the development of intuitive and fine-grained control of neuroprosthetics, requiring neural signals of individual digits.
evidence: This is a speculative application of the findings.

claim: Digit topography can be identified in humans using high-field neuroimaging with high inter- and intra-subject reliability.
source: Using high-field neuroimaging, it is now possible to identify these characteristic digit maps in humans, with high inter- and intra-subject reliability (Ejaz et al., 2015; Kolasinski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Digit topography is characterised by digit selectivity.
source: Digit topography is characterised in neuroimaging by two main principles: digit selectivity (Kolasinski et al., 2016) and inter-digit overlap (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Digit topography is characterised by inter-digit overlap.
source: Digit topography is characterised in neuroimaging by two main principles: digit selectivity (Kolasinski et al., 2016) and inter-digit overlap (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Digits used more frequently together in daily life benefit from increased representational overlap.
source: These maps are thought to be shaped and maintained by daily life experience: digits used more frequently together in daily life benefit from increased representational overlap (Ejaz et al., 2015), and following single digit amputation remaining digits' topography changes (Merzenich et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Following single digit amputation, remaining digits' topography changes.
source: These maps are thought to be shaped and maintained by daily life experience: digits used more frequently together in daily life benefit from increased representational overlap (Ejaz et al., 2015), and following single digit amputation remaining digits' topography changes (Merzenich et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Amputees commonly experience lingering sensations from their amputated body part.
source: Amputees commonly experience lingering sensations from their amputated body part (Flor and Nikolajsen, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Phantom sensations are best described as a vivid sensation of the missing hand as if it is still present.
source: Phantom sensations are not necessarily painful, and are best described as a vivid sensation of the missing hand as if it is still present (Flor and Nikolajsen, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: When instructed to move their phantom hand, amputees report detailed kinaesthetic sensations regarding the extent of movement afforded by different phantom digits.
source: When instructed to move their phantom hand, amputees report detailed kinaesthetic sensations regarding the extent of movement afforded by different phantom digits.
evidence: This is based on reported observations from amputees.

claim: Phantom movements are known to evoke signals in the sensorimotor system.
source: Phantom movements are known to evoke signals in the sensorimotor system (Makin et al., 2013a; Reilly et al., 2006; Raffin et al., 2012b), previously attributed to abnormal processing caused by the amputation (e.g. aberrant inputs (Makin et al., 2013a), peripheral reorganisation (Reilly et al., 2006)).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phantom movement-evoked signals have been previously attributed to abnormal processing caused by the amputation.
source: Phantom movements are known to evoke signals in the sensorimotor system (Makin et al., 2013a; Reilly et al., 2006; Raffin et al., 2012b), previously attributed to abnormal processing caused by the amputation (e.g. aberrant inputs (Makin et al., 2013a), peripheral reorganisation (Reilly et al., 2006)).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The study used ultra high-field 7 tesla neuroimaging in two individuals who lost their left hand several decades ago (25 and 31 years post amputation).
source: To study phantom digit topography, we used ultra high-field 7 tesla neuroimaging in two individuals who lost their left hand several decades ago (25 and 31 years post amputation) and eleven right-handed controls.
evidence: This describes the methodology and participants of the study.

claim: Both amputees reported exceptionally vivid kinaesthetic phantom sensations during individual digit movements.
source: Both amputees reported exceptionally vivid kinaesthetic phantom sensations during individual digit movements (see Figure 1—source data 1, 2, for clinical and demographic details).
evidence: This is based on self-report data from the amputees.

claim: Phantom movements are distinguishable from imagined movements.
source: Importantly, phantom movements are distinguishable from imagined movements.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical evidence.

claim: Phantom limb movements elicit both central and peripheral motor signals that are different from those found during imagined movements.
source: This is supported by empirical evidence demonstrating that phantom limb movements elicit both central and peripheral motor signals, that are different from those found during imagined movements (Makin et al., 2013a; Reilly et al., 2006; Raffin et al., 2012b, 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both amputees showed a clear gradient of digit preference in the central sulcus and postcentral gyrus.
source: Similarly, both amputees showed a clear gradient of digit preference in the central sulcus and postcentral gyrus (Figure 1B; see Figure 1—figure supplement 3 for intact hand maps).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the neuroimaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The position, digit order, and extent of the missing hand maps were qualitatively similar to those observed in controls.
source: Qualitatively, the position, digit order, and extent of the missing hand maps were similar to those observed in controls.
evidence: This is based on qualitative comparison of the neuroimaging data.

claim: Digit selectivity in amputees was consistent, though reduced compared to controls.
source: Analysis of spatial correspondence of 'same' versus 'different' digit clusters between two halves of the dataset further confirmed that while reduced (compared to controls), digit selectivity in amputees was consistent (Figure 1D; see Materials and methods for further details).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the split-half consistency analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Amputees showed lower split-half consistency for 'same'-digit clusters compared to controls.
source: Amputees showed lower split-half consistency for 'same'-digit clusters (averaged across digits) compared to controls (95% confidence intervals (CI) = 0.43–0.68, as assessed using a bootstrap approach).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neuroimaging data.

claim: Amputees' 'same'-digit clusters were more consistent than 'different'-digit clusters in controls.
source: However, amputees' 'same'-digit clusters were more consistent than 'different'-digit clusters in controls (i.e. fell outside the CI of 'different'-digit clusters split-half consistency in controls), indicating that although reduced, the digit maps of the amputees were consistent.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neuroimaging data.

claim: Both amputees showed maps in the hemisphere contralateral to the intact hand, dissociated from a second map in the missing hand hemisphere.
source: Both amputees showed maps in the hemisphere contralateral to the intact hand, dissociated from a second map in the missing hand hemisphere (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the bimanual task neuroimaging data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The bimanual missing hand map corresponded to the original unimanual missing hand map.
source: The latter map corresponded to the original (unimanual movements, Figure 1) missing hand map, as confirmed by higher spatial correspondence for 'same' (average Dice overlap coefficient: 0.49, 0.40 for above and below elbow amputees) versus 'different' (0.06, 0.04) digit clusters across the two (unimanual and bimanual) missing hand datasets (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spatial correspondence analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The missing hand topography is independent from the representation of the intact hand.
source: This result also demonstrates the independence of the missing hand topography from the representation of the intact hand.
evidence: This is inferred from the bimanual task results showing dissociated maps.

claim: Following unilateral arm amputation, the intact hand becomes over-represented in the missing hand territory.
source: Our group and others previously showed that following unilateral arm amputation, the intact hand becomes over-represented in the missing hand territory (Makin et al., 2013b; Philip and Frey, 2014; Raffin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The digit map in the missing hand territory is not driven by an emerging representation of the intact hand.
source: Our results therefore confirm that the digit map in the missing hand territory is not driven by an emerging representation of the intact hand.
evidence: This is inferred from the bimanual task results.

claim: The preserved missing hand topography can co-occur with remapping of body parts.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, this study's participants showed over-representation of their intact hand in the missing hand territory, indicating that the preserved missing hand topography can co-occur with remapping of body parts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both amputees showed greater average overlap across digits compared to controls.
source: In general, both amputees showed greater average overlap across digits (0.55 and 0.54 for above and below elbow amputees respectively), compared to controls (95% confidence intervals (CI) = 0.24–0.41).
evidence: This is based on inter-digit representational similarity analysis.

claim: Both amputees demonstrated typical inter-digit overlap patterns in the missing hand map.
source: However, when examining the inter-digit overlap pattern in the missing hand map, both amputees demonstrated typical patterns (Figure 3A,C; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for intact hand).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the inter-digit similarity matrices shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Each amputee's inter-digit overlap pattern showed high correlation with the controls.
source: This was reflected in high correlation between each amputee's inter-digit overlap pattern and the controls, as assessed using a bootstrapping approach (average rs = 0.61 and rs = 0.78, 95% CI = 0.25–0.89 and 95% CI = 0.62–0.90 for above and below elbow amputees respectively).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the inter-digit overlap patterns.

claim: The average amputee-to-controls Spearman correlation values fell within the controls-to-controls Spearman correlation range.
source: These average amputee-to-controls Spearman correlation values fell well within the controls-to-controls Spearman correlation range (95% CI = 0.35–0.95; Figure 3C), providing further evidence for characteristic missing hand representation decades after amputation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A third amputee with brachial plexus avulsion showed digit preference for the missing hand in the postcentral gyrus and central sulcus.
source: Using the bimanual task specified above (Figure 4A) we identified digit preference for the missing hand in the postcentral gyrus and central sulcus (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the neuroimaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The brachial plexus amputee showed a typical inter-digit overlap pattern.
source: We also identified a typical inter-digit overlap pattern (Figure 4D), as confirmed in comparison with the control population described in Figure 3 (average Spearman correlation with controls = 0.76, with 95% CI = 0.30–0.92).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the inter-digit similarity matrix shown in Figure 4D and statistical comparison.

claim: Preserved digit topography exists independently of peripheral inputs.
source: Together, these results suggest that preserved representation of the missing hand existed independently of peripheral inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the brachial plexus amputee results.

claim: The functional digit layout of S1 prevails following arm amputation.
source: Together we show that, although the missing hand maps were weaker and noisier than the maps found in controls, the functional digit layout of S1 prevails following arm amputation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental data.

claim: Digit topography was detectable despite decades without organised peripheral inputs associated with normal hand function.
source: Digit topography, previously thought to depend on experience (Ejaz et al., 2015; Merzenich et al., 1984), was detectable despite decades without organised peripheral inputs associated with normal hand function.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings and challenges previous assumptions.

claim: The findings call for a reassessment of the role of sensory input in regulating brain organisation and plasticity.
source: Our findings call for a reassessment of the role of sensory input in regulating brain organisation and plasticity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications of the findings.

claim: Following arm amputation, the missing hand territory in S1 is taken over by representations of other body parts.
source: For example, following arm amputation, the missing hand territory in S1 is taken over by representations of other body parts (e.g. the neighbouring representation of the face in monkeys [Pons et al., 1991], or the intact hand in humans [Makin et al., 2013b]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Following macular degeneration, the functional representation of the intact visual field was unchanged.
source: For example following macular degeneration, the functional representation of the intact visual field was unchanged ([Baseler et al., 2011], see [Smirnakis et al., 2005] for similar results in non-human primates).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reorganisation in the missing hand territory following input loss does not abolish the original functional layout in sensory cortex.
source: Here we show that reorganisation in the missing hand territory following input loss does not abolish the original functional layout in sensory cortex.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Reorganisation following sensory input loss does not exclude the possibility for simultaneous preservation of the original function of that region.
source: Already in their seal work Merzenich et al. suggested that reorganisation following sensory input loss does not exclude the possibility for simultaneous preservation of the original function of that region (Merzenich et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The capacity for S1 reorganisation is more limited than initially thought.
source: Accordingly, recent structural and functional evidence shows that the capacity for S1 reorganisation is more limited than initially thought, and that instead the functional changes previously observed in S1 following input loss could be attributed to reorganisation in sub-cortical areas in the afferent pathway, principally the brainstem (Jain et al., 1998; Kambi et al., 2014; Chand and Jain, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Functional changes previously observed in S1 following input loss could be attributed to reorganisation in sub-cortical areas in the afferent pathway, principally the brainstem.
source: Accordingly, recent structural and functional evidence shows that the capacity for S1 reorganisation is more limited than initially thought, and that instead the functional changes previously observed in S1 following input loss could be attributed to reorganisation in sub-cortical areas in the afferent pathway, principally the brainstem (Jain et al., 1998; Kambi et al., 2014; Chand and Jain, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Previous findings of massive cortical reorganisation in S1 reflect reorganisation of inputs, rather than reorganisation within S1 itself.
source: In other words, previous findings of massive cortical reorganisation in S1 reflect reorganisation of inputs, rather than reorganisation within S1 itself.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on recent evidence cited.

claim: In the below elbow amputee, some forearm muscles normally controlling hand movements are spared and therefore proprioceptive inputs relating to phantom hand movements likely persist.
source: In the below elbow amputee, some forearm muscles normally controlling hand movements are spared and therefore proprioceptive inputs relating to phantom hand movements likely persist (Nyström and Hagbarth, 1981).
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: In the above elbow amputee, proprioceptive inputs from forearm muscles would be absent.
source: In the above elbow amputee, these inputs would be absent, though ectopic firing from the injured nerve (Nyström and Hagbarth, 1981) or intact dorsal root ganglia could preserve some afferent inputs (as previously shown following peripheral nerve injury [Nordin et al., 1984], see also [Vaso et al., 2014] for related findings).
evidence: This is inferred from the level of amputation and anatomical knowledge.

claim: Ectopic firing from the injured nerve or intact dorsal root ganglia could preserve some afferent inputs in the above elbow amputee.
source: In the above elbow amputee, these inputs would be absent, though ectopic firing from the injured nerve (Nyström and Hagbarth, 1981) or intact dorsal root ganglia could preserve some afferent inputs (as previously shown following peripheral nerve injury [Nordin et al., 1984], see also [Vaso et al., 2014] for related findings).
evidence: This is a speculative possibility supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the amputee suffering from brachial plexus avulsion injury, the dorsal root ganglia are damaged, meaning that no peripheral input should be available.
source: However, in the amputee suffering from brachial plexus avulsion injury, the dorsal root ganglia are damaged, meaning that no such peripheral input should be available.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the injury and its anatomical consequences.

claim: The preserved missing hand maps are highly probable to not be maintained by peripheral input, but rather are driven by processing in the central nervous system itself.
source: Given the observation of preserved topography in all three cases, it is highly probable that the preserved missing hand maps are not maintained by peripheral input, but rather are driven by processing in the central nervous system itself.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of preserved topography across different amputation types.

claim: The motor system is thought to provide information about its descending commands to the sensory system, by means of efference copy.
source: The motor system is thought to provide information about its descending commands to the sensory system, by means of efference copy.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in motor control theory.

claim: When efference signals reach the sensory areas, they evoke activity in those areas.
source: When efference signals reach the sensory areas, they evoke activity in those areas.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in motor control theory.

claim: The pattern of corollary discharge could resemble that of the sensory feedback to be expected from the movement.
source: The pattern of this corollary discharge could resemble that of the sensory feedback to be expected from the movement (London and Miller, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Predictive signals are fundamental components for current theories of motor control.
source: While predictive signals are fundamental components for current theories of motor control (Franklin and Wolpert, 2011), surprisingly little empirical evidence exists to demonstrate efferent signals in the primates' S1 hand representation independently of afferent processing (London and Miller, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Surprisingly little empirical evidence exists to demonstrate efferent signals in the primates' S1 hand representation independently of afferent processing.
source: While predictive signals are fundamental components for current theories of motor control (Franklin and Wolpert, 2011), surprisingly little empirical evidence exists to demonstrate efferent signals in the primates' S1 hand representation independently of afferent processing (London and Miller, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Evidence for digit topography in S1 despite the physical absence of a hand suggests the involvement of non-afferent processing in S1.
source: Our evidence for digit topography in S1 despite the physical absence of a hand suggests the involvement of non-afferent processing in S1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The persistence of efference signals from the motor system could contribute to the maintenance of preserved information content in SI despite afferent input loss.
source: The persistence of efference signals from the motor system could contribute to the maintenance of preserved information content in SI despite afferent input loss.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings.

claim: All tested amputees reported experiencing exceptionally vivid phantom sensations, allowing them to voluntarily move each of their phantom fingers.
source: Our findings are based on the unique phenomenology of phantom sensations, and as such all tested amputees reported experiencing exceptionally vivid phantom sensations, allowing them to voluntarily move each of their phantom fingers.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the study participants.

claim: Phantom hand movements activate the missing hand territory in individuals experiencing varying levels of phantom sensation vividness.
source: Our previous findings, showing that phantom hand movements activate the missing hand territory in individuals experiencing varying levels of phantom sensation vividness (Makin et al., 2013a; 2015) might indicate that this is a general phenomenon.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Previous studies do not provide information on whether the topographic features underlying the phantom-evoked activity were preserved.
source: However, we note that these previous studies do not provide information on whether the topographic features underlying the phantom-evoked activity were preserved.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors regarding previous work.

claim: The notion of brain reorganisation has posed an unexpected obstacle to recent technological developments of human-technology fusion, i.e. neuroprosthetics.
source: The notion of brain reorganisation has posed an unexpected obstacle to recent technological developments of human-technology fusion, i.e. neuroprosthetics.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of challenges in neuroprosthetics development.

claim: Neuroprosthetics allow patients with sensorimotor impairments to directly interface with a robotic limb using cortical signals of the hand.
source: Neuroprosthetics allow patients with sensorimotor impairments (e.g. amputation, paralysis) to directly interface with a robotic limb using cortical signals of the hand.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of neuroprosthetics technology.

claim: The relevant information necessary for intuitive neuroprosthesis control may not be attainable once input is lost and functional reorganisation occurs.
source: However, the relevant information necessary for intuitive neuroprosthesis control may not be attainable once input is lost and functional reorganisation occurs.
evidence: This is a concern based on the assumption of reorganisation.

claim: The finding of persistence of topography despite input loss could be exploited to develop intuitive fine-grained control of neuroprosthetics in disabled populations.
source: By demonstrating persistence of topography despite input loss, our finding could be exploited to develop intuitive fine-grained control of neuroprosthetics (Bensmaia and Miller, 2014) (e.g. requiring representation of individual digits) in disabled populations.
evidence: This is a speculative application of the findings.

claim: The study initially screened 63 unilateral upper-limb amputees.
source: We initially screened 63 unilateral upper-limb amputees, of which 22 met the initial criteria for MRI safety.
evidence: This describes the participant recruitment process.

claim: Eight amputees met the criterion for vividness of kinaesthetic sensations while volitionally moving each of their phantom digits.
source: Eight amputees met our 2nd criterion for vividness of kinaesthetic sensations while volitionally moving each of their phantom digits.
evidence: This describes the participant recruitment process.

claim: Only two of the candidates were approved for undergoing ultra high-field (7 tesla) MRI.
source: Only two of these candidates were approved for undergoing ultra high-field (7 tesla) MRI, based on institute's standard operating procedures for MRI safety.
evidence: This describes the participant recruitment process and safety constraints.

claim: All three amputees included in the study were amputated on their left arm due to a trauma and were right-hand dominant prior to the amputation.
source: All three amputees included in the study were amputated on their left arm due to a trauma and were right-hand dominant prior to the amputation (based on self report).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the study participants.

claim: A group of thirteen two-handed control participants with a dominant right hand were recruited to take part in the study.
source: In addition, a group of thirteen two-handed control participants with a dominant right hand were recruited to take part in the study (mean age ± s.e.m. = 43 ± 3; three females).
evidence: This describes the control participants.

claim: Volitional movement of a phantom hand elicits both central and peripheral motor signals that are different from those found during imagined movements.
source: Volitional (and not necessarily painful) movement of a phantom hand elicits both central (Makin et al., 2013a; Raffin et al., 2012b; Makin et al., 2015; Reilly and Sirigu, 2008) and peripheral motor signals (Reilly et al., 2006; Raffin et al., 2012a; Reilly and Sirigu, 2008) that are different from those found during imagined movements.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Amputees and controls showed activation in primary somatosensory and motor cortex during hand movements.
source: Amputees and controls showed activation in primary somatosensory and motor cortex (S1 and M1, respectively; left panel), as well as in the supplementary motor area (SMA, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the activation maps shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Phantom hand movements activate a network of brain areas normally associated with hand movement.
source: These results show that phantom hand movements activate a network of brain areas normally associated with hand movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the activation patterns shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Two of the tested amputees show over-representation of their intact hand in the missing hand territory.
source: The above elbow and brachial plexus amputees showed significantly lower asymmetry than controls (one-tailed Crawford and Howell t-test [Corballis, 2009]; t(14) = −1.84, p = 0.04; and t(14) = −1.96, p = 0.04 respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the asymmetry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The missing hand maps can be preserved while reorganisation of displaced inputs from the intact hand has taken place.
source: These results suggest that the missing hand maps can be preserved while reorganisation of displaced inputs from the intact hand has taken place.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-occurrence of preserved topography and intact hand over-representation.

claim: The organisation, extent and consistency of the digit maps qualitatively resembled the left (missing) hand maps found in both controls and amputees.
source: Note that the organisation, extent and consistency of the digit maps qualitatively resembled the left (missing) hand maps (obtained using self-paced digit flexion and extension) found in both controls and amputees (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on qualitative comparison of the intact hand maps with the missing hand maps.

claim: Brachial plexus avulsion injury involves the tearing of the nerve from its attachment at the spinal cord, abolishing afferent inputs and efferent outputs to the residual limb.
source: This injury involves the tearing of the nerve from its attachment at the spinal cord, abolishing afferent inputs and efferent outputs to the residual limb.
evidence: This is based on medical knowledge of the injury.

claim: Only one of the three tested amputees reporting to suffer from brachial plexus avulsion injury was unable to detect any of the stimuli on the residual arm.
source: Only one of the three tested amputees reporting to suffer from brachial plexus avulsion injury was unable to detect any of the stimuli on the residual arm.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data.

claim: The brachial plexus amputee who could not detect stimuli also did not reveal a change in the EMG channels induced by cued phantom hand movements.
source: This participant also did not reveal a change in the EMG channels induced by cued phantom hand movements.
evidence: This is based on EMG testing data.

claim: The travelling wave approach has previously been well-validated for sensory body mapping.
source: This approach has previously been well-validated for sensory body mapping (Kolasinski et al., 2016; Mancini et al., 2012; Orlov et al., 2010; Sanchez-Panchuelo et al., 2010; Sereno and Huang, 2006; Zeharia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous validation studies.

claim: The winner-takes-all analysis makes the travelling wave approach insensitive to overlapping cortical digit representations.
source: Whereas the travelling wave approach provides detailed information regarding digit preference, the winner-takes-all analysis (see below) makes this approach insensitive to overlapping cortical digit representations.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the analysis method's limitations.

claim: Regions activated by multiple digits will be difficult to identify using a standard GLM when the paradigm involves continuous cycles of digit movements with no interruption of baseline periods.
source: Moreover, as the paradigm involves continuous cycles of digit movements with no interruption of baseline periods, regions activated by multiple digits will be difficult to identify using a standard GLM (Besle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of GLM limitations and supported by a citation.
